quote: Save 500 lives, with 90% probability; save no lives, 10% probability.
content: The essay's version of this problem has unequal expected values, 450 lives against 400. No study is cited showing that "most people choose option 1" under that design. In the problem it is adapted from, Tversky & Kahneman's "Asian disease" (Tversky & Kahneman 1981), the two options have equal expected values. That is what makes the framing effect a clean test of inconsistency rather than of attitude to risk. Changing the numbers while keeping the reported result substitutes the author's prediction for data.

quote: Then a majority choose option 2. Even though it’s the same gamble.
content: The underlying framing effect is one of the most robust results in the field. In the original version, with equal expected values, the preference reversal between the "saved" and "die" framings replicated strongly across 36 laboratories in the first Many Labs project (Klein et al. 2014). Whatever one concludes about "shut up and multiply," the inconsistency the essay describes is real.

quote: (Lives saved don’t diminish in marginal utility, so this is an appropriate calculation.)
content: This is contestable, not a technicality. Diamond (1967) showed that caring how risk is distributed, giving everyone a fair chance rather than letting the lottery fall on the same people, violates the sure-thing principle and can't be captured by expected lives saved. Public risk policy routinely treats catastrophic, correlated losses as worse than the same expected number of independent deaths. The parenthesis settles by decree one of the two questions that make this example hard.

quote: on pain of decision-theoretic incoherence, there must be some number of hiccups that would add up to rival the negative value of a shark attack
content: No coherence theorem requires this. Lexicographic preferences, which rank a shark attack strictly worse than any number of hiccups, are complete and transitive. They violate only the continuity (Archimedean) axiom, which is a structural assumption rather than a condition of coherence, and they can be represented by lexicographic utilities (Fishburn 1974). There are serious arguments against lexical views. Spectrum arguments lead step by step from one severe harm to many slightly lesser ones, but they force a choice between transitivity and aggregation that philosophers haven't resolved (Temkin, Rethinking the Good, 2012; book, no DOI). "On pain of incoherence" presents one side of that dilemma as a theorem.

quote: My favorite anecdote along these lines comes from a team of researchers who evaluated the effectiveness of a certain project
content: The anecdote is unsourced, and the generalization it implies is false. US regulatory agencies routinely put a dollar value on statistical lives. The EPA, the Department of Transportation and others use values around ten million dollars or more in cost–benefit analysis, drawn from a large literature of labor-market estimates (Viscusi & Aldy 2003). Governments do refuse some trade-offs, and taboo trade-offs are real (Tetlock et al. 2000). But one agency's refusal is not evidence that "you couldn't put a dollar value on human life" governs policy.

quote: If you’re doing it for the spiritual benefit, that is nothing but selfishness.
content: This sits oddly with "Not for the Sake of Happiness (Alone)," which argued that valuing your own experience alongside its objects isn't selfishness. Most real motives are mixed. Donors who enjoy giving still give, and people who feel good about helping help more, not less. The warm glow Andreoni (1990) modeled is one reason people give at all. Condemning it as "nothing but selfishness" is a moral judgment the book's own analysis of motives doesn't support.
